Nestled within a natural amphitheatre formed by a convergence of mountain ranges, this body of water sits at the meeting point of atmospheric forces that produce a phenomenon unlike anywhere else recorded on earth. Each night, warm moisture-laden air rising from the warm surface below collides with cold descending air channelled down from the surrounding peaks. The result is an electrical storm of extraordinary frequency and intensity — recorded on approximately 260 days in a given year — so reliable that sailors once used it as a navigational beacon. It has its own name in meteorological literature. The lake's unique identity in this regard is now formally recognised as a world record.
